findings.message: The story's core accessibility design goal (no recurring/tracked noun or verb contains b, d, p or q) is broken by two heavily repeated, plot-central words. 'steps'/'step' (the escape route the whole plot is built around; 10 occurrences across 8 passages, e.g. path-b-find: 'The steps will show the way out.', climax-clock: 'showing steps down and out.', ending-1, ending-5) contains 'p'. 'second' used as 'a second gate' (the alternate exit, central to endings 1, 2 and 3; opening: 'for one second', climax: 'a second, smaller lock', ending-1: 'a second gate', ending-2: 'the second gate', ending-3: 'a second gate') contains 'd'. continuity.facts in brief.json explicitly (and incorrectly) asserts 'the steps' already avoids b/d/p/q, and the brief's own closed-syllable-words word set mandates 'steps' (schemas/brief wordSets, closed-syllable-words), so this looks like a brief-level contradiction that the narrative-designer could not have avoided while also satisfying the literacy word-set requirement -- recommend escalating to product-architect/continuity to resolve the brief before the draft can satisfy the stated design goal.

Inconsistent item tracking: path-a-find (and the repeated detour-item) narrate 'Inside sat an old rusty key and a worn coin' but only 'rusty-key' is ever added via effects.addItems -- the coin is never registered as a carried item. Ending-2 then narrates 'The old coin fell from his hand and was gone' as if the party had been carrying it the whole time, with no passage showing anyone taking the coin. A reader tracking items/clues (the review focus for consistency) cannot explain where the coin came from or why only Theo had it.

reports/validation.r2.json brief check reports '1 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 13-word limit'. Manually re-reading every sentence in the draft, each individual sentence is under 13 words; the only candidate is the quoted dialogue in path-a-find ('Finn said, \'This must unlock something.\' Suri put the key in her coat.') which a naive sentence splitter merges into one 14-word unit across a quotation mark. Likely a tokenizer artifact rather than a real prose defect, but worth confirming with app-engineer/literacy-specialist.

detour-item and detour-clue repeat the chest/note text from path-a-find and path-b-find almost verbatim ('a rusty key and a worn coin ... faint shine in the torch light'; the full Wren note text) rather than giving fresh prose for the second visit. This does not force the reader to re-read an already-seen page (these are distinct passage ids and the graph has no edges back into previously visited nodes, confirmed in reports/graph.r2.json), so it is not a reread violation, but it is weak craft and it is the same spot where the untracked-coin inconsistency above repeats a second time.

drafts/story.r2.json literacy.wordSets[1] ("closed-syllable-words") is missing the "concept" field that brief.json and word-weave-plan.json both carry for this set (concept: "closed-syllable"). Because src/literacy/analyzer.ts only runs the per-word spelling-pattern check when a word set names a concept (conceptMismatches: concept ? set.words.filter(w => !concept.detect(w)) : []), the whole-set mismatch check never ran for this set and silently reported conceptMismatches: [] in reports/literacy.r2.json/.md and automatedChecks 'word-set-concepts-match-spelling'. This let a real defect through: re-running the actual closed-syllable detector from src/literacy/taxonomy.ts against this exact word list gives key=false, stage=false, exit=false, gate=false, coin=false (only lock, chest, steps, clock match). Five of the nine target words for the declared 'closed-syllable' concept do not carry a closed-syllable spelling pattern at all: 'key' is a long-vowel vowel-team/y-as-vowel word (not closed), 'gate' and 'stage' are silent-e / vowel-consonant-e syllables (confirmed independently -- both appear as examples under the report's own 'silent-e' concept match list), 'coin' is an oi vowel-team/diphthong word, and 'exit' is two syllables (ex-it) so it falls outside this single-syllable detector and is a materially harder decoding task than the one-vowel closed-syllable words it is grouped with. A dyslexic reader drilling this labelled set (e.g. in path-a-find: 'The key had a faint shine in the torch light.'; the-gate: 'the old lock sat shut tight'; climax-clock: 'the hands moved to the hour') would be told these words share one decoding pattern when they do not. This is the acceptance-gate condition for changes-requested ('a word-set word does not carry the declared pattern'). Fix requires either (a) restoring the concept field so the gate re-runs and fails loudly, and (b) the narrative-designer/product-architect choosing a word-weave-plan word list for the closed-syllable set that is phonetically consistent (true single-syllable closed-syllable words such as lock, chest, steps, clock, plus replacements for key/gate/stage/coin/exit), since swapping words also changes which other taxonomy concept those replaced words would need to serve instead.

The brief's own dyslexia-specific design goal (continuity.facts: 'the lock, the key, the chest, the stage, the steps, the gate, the clock, the coin, rush, shut, wish ... contain no letter b, d, p or q') is false for 'steps'/'step' as written: s-t-e-p-s contains a 'p'. The word appears 16 times across both singular and plural forms on passages that sit on the route to every ending (e.g. path-b-find: '"The steps will show the way out."'; climax-clock: 'showing steps down and out'; ending-1: 'went down the secret steps'; ending-5 implicitly via 'sat on the steps'), so this is not a one-off slip but the story's central tracked escape-route object, repeated on every route, carrying exactly the kind of letter a dyslexic reader is asked never to have to hold in memory while decoding a plot-critical word. I confirm qa-engineer's review-1-qa finding on this point (plus their 'second'/'a second gate' catch) from the literacy side: this is a brief-level contradiction, not something the narrative-designer could have avoided while still meeting the word-weave-plan's requirement to use 'steps' as a closed-syllable-words target word. Escalate to product-architect/continuity to resolve the brief (either drop the b/d/p/q claim for 'steps' and acknowledge it as an accepted, deliberate single exception, or replace 'steps' in both the continuity facts and the closed-syllable word set with a genuinely p/b/d/q-free closed-syllable word and rebalance occurrence counts).

path-a-shelf introduces 'rod' ('A thin rod sat inside, set at an angle.' / 'Tug the thin rod slowly') as a new object noun containing 'd'. It is not tracked as an item and is confined to one optional branch, so it is low-impact, but it is mentioned twice rather than the single one-off mention the brief's avoid-list asks for when a new b/d/p/q word is unavoidable.

reports/literacy.r2.json's automated 'sentence-length' check uses a fixed 20-word threshold, not the brief's maxSentenceWords: 13. I hand-counted every sentence in drafts/story.r2.json and found none over 13 words (longest is the 13-word 'Theo ran to the gate, the main exit, and gave it a tug.' in the opening passage), so there is no current violation, but the automated check as configured would not catch a future 14-20 word sentence against this brief's tighter limit. Flagging only as a detection-limit note, consistent with qa-engineer's separate tokenizer-artifact note on reports/validation.r2.json.

Skills practised: read start to finish on any route, this story gives practice in decoding short-vowel closed-syllable words and the sh digraph in natural sentence context (lock, chest, steps, clock, shelf, flash, crash, rush, hush, shut all recur across the opening, both search branches, the gathering, the gate, the climax and all five endings); recognising and re-encountering the same small set of plot-critical words repeatedly builds sight-word fluency for exactly those words. The branching clue-and-inventory structure (finding the key, finding Wren's note, choosing whether to set the clock or turn the key first) gives practice in sequencing a short set of ordered steps and in inference (working out that the key and the note are meant to be used together, and what happens if a step is skipped or done out of order). The short glossary entries (theater, curious, furious, founder, castellan) with syllable breakdowns support vocabulary growth from context rather than requiring the reader to stop and look words up elsewhere.

Limits of automated detection: reports/literacy.r2.json and reports/literacy.r2.md both state their method plainly -- deterministic token counts plus ORTHOGRAPHIC (spelling-pattern) detectors, not phonological ones. A detector match means a word's letters fit a regex, not that a human has confirmed the sound a reader would actually produce ('ea' matches both 'bread' and 'bead'). This revision is a clear illustration of why that distinction matters in practice: the automated 'word-set-concepts-match-spelling' check reported no mismatches for the closed-syllable-words set only because a required 'concept' field was missing from the draft (see the first major finding above), and even the real detector only checks spelling -- it took a human judgement call to confirm that 'key', 'gate', 'stage', 'coin' and 'exit' do not actually sound like the closed-syllable words they are grouped with. Minimum-occurrence counts, every-word-used and per-route coverage, by contrast, are reliable deterministic counts; I independently spot-checked those against the draft text and they are not in question. I am an AI-assisted reviewer, not a certified literacy professional; a qualified human should confirm the phonological judgements in this review before publication.

The core accessibility design goal in metadata.theme and brief.json continuity.facts ('no recurring/tracked noun or verb contains b, d, p or q') is still broken by the word 'steps'/'step' (contains 'p'), unchanged since revision 2. This is the escape-route object the whole plot is built around: wren-note/path-b-find/detour-clue quote the clue 'The steps will show the way out.'; climax-clock says 'showing steps down and out'; ending-1 ('went down the secret steps'), ending-2 ('rushed down the new steps'), and ending-5 ('sat on the steps and waited') all repeat it -- 16 occurrences total across 8+ passages. revision-notes.r3.md (section 4, 'note, not fixed') explicitly says this half of the original r2 major finding was deliberately left unresolved and escalated to product-architect, because brief.json's own closed-syllable-words word set mandates >=30 occurrences of 'steps' while brief.json continuity.facts simultaneously (and incorrectly) asserts 'the steps' contains no b/d/p/q. I confirm brief.json is still unchanged on this point as of revision 4 (continuity.facts still lists 'the steps' among the letter-clean words, and the closed-syllable-words set still requires 'steps' with minOccurrences 30) -- revision 3/4 only fixed the 'second gate' half of the original bundled finding, never the 'steps' half. Only the coin-tracking finding and the 'second gate' finding from review-1-qa.r2.json are actually resolved; this part of that same finding remains open and needs a brief-level fix (drop 'steps' from the mandated word set, or amend continuity.facts to admit the exception) before it can be resolved in prose.

Ending-5 ('Wait Out the Storm') does not reliably match the setup. At 'threshold', the 'try-alone' choice (target ending-5) is never locked and carries no requires/lockedHint tied to inventory, so a reader who already picked up both the rusty key (path-a-find or detour-item) and Wren's note (path-b-find or detour-clue) before reaching threshold can still choose it. Yet ending-5's text asserts the opposite of that reader's actual state: 'Without the key and the note, the lock would not give way' and 'They never did find Wren Castellan's secret way out. Next time, they would look for the note and the key first.' Traced route: opening -> go-stage -> path-a -> check-shelf -> path-a-shelf -> shove-back -> path-a-find (has-item) -> keep-key-a -> gathering -> back-clue -> detour-clue (has-clue) -> with-note-a -> the-gate -> shine-torch -> threshold -> try-alone -> ending-5. On this route the reader holds both tracked items (visible in the inventory UI) while the ending narrates that they never had them. This is a content-integrity defect in a reachable ending, not merely a flavour choice.

reports/validation.r4.json brief check still reports '1 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 13-word limit', unchanged since revision 2/3. Re-reading every sentence in the draft manually, each individual sentence is under 13 words; the only candidate is the quoted dialogue in path-a-find ('Finn said, 'This must unlock something.' Suri put the key in her coat.'), which a naive sentence splitter likely merges across the quotation mark into one longer unit. Still looks like a tokenizer artifact rather than a real prose defect (brief.ok remains true, it is a warning only), but it has now persisted across three revisions without confirmation from app-engineer/literacy-specialist.

'rod' in path-a-shelf ('A thin rod sat inside, set at an angle.' / 'Tug the thin rod slowly') contains 'd'. It is not a brief-mandated, repeated, or tracked word (used twice, only inside this single optional branch, not carried as an item or referenced elsewhere), so it does not meet the bar of the other major finding above, but it is worth the narrative-designer's awareness given how sensitive this story's premise is to the b/d/p/q rule.

The split fixed from revision 2 is genuinely correct this time, independently re-derived, not just trusted from reports/literacy.r4.json. brief.json and drafts/story.r4.json literacy.wordSets now declare closed-syllable-words (concept closed-syllable, words lock/chest/steps/clock, minOccurrences 30) and a separate castle-key-words (no concept field, words key/stage/exit/gate/coin, minOccurrences 40). I ran each word by hand through src/literacy/taxonomy.ts's actual detect() regex for 'closed-syllable' (/^[^aeiouy]*[aeiou][^aeiouy]+$/.test(w) && w.length<=6 && !/igh|[aeiou]r|a(ll|lk)/.test(w)): lock -> l+o+ck, true; chest -> ch+e+st, true; steps -> st+e+ps, true; clock -> cl+o+ck, true. All four genuinely carry the closed-syllable pattern, unlike r2 where key/stage/exit/gate/coin were wrongly folded into this same concept. For castle-key-words I confirmed why no single concept fits: gate and stage both match silent-e (vowel-consonant-e: g-a-t-e, st-a-g-e), key is a vowel-team-adjacent 'ey' spelling not in the taxonomy's vowel-team list, exit is two syllables (ex-it) so the single-syllable closed-syllable detector correctly rejects it, and coin is an 'oi' diphthong not in the taxonomy's vowel-team pattern list (ai ay ee ea oa oe ie igh ue). Leaving this set concept-less is the honest choice, not a workaround. reports/literacy.r4.json's word-set-concepts-match-spelling: true and conceptMismatches: [] for all three sets agree with my independent check. I also hand re-ran digraph-sh's w.includes('sh') against all nine sh-words words (wish, shine, flash, crash, shelf, rush, hush, shut, shock) and all contain 'sh'. The r2 defect is resolved.

Unresolved carry-over from my own revision-2 review (review-2-literacy.r2.json, finding 2), confirmed again independently on r4 and still not fixed: brief.json's continuity.facts claims the story's recurring, tracked nouns and verbs (lock, key, chest, stage, steps, gate, clock, coin, rush, shut, wish) 'contain no letter b, d, p or q,' but 'steps' literally contains a 'p' (s-t-e-p-s), and its singular 'step' does too. This is the story's own stated dyslexia-design premise (brief.json's theme: a reader who is still unsure of b/d/p/q 'should not have to hold a main character's name or a repeated plot object in working memory while also decoding it'), and 'steps'/'step' is exactly such a repeated plot object: it is one of only four words in the heavily-weighted closed-syllable-words set (minOccurrences 30), occurs 10 times in the current prose (steps: 10, per reports/literacy.r4.json perWord and my own grep), and sits on the shortest route to every ending (opening and the-gate, both universal, plus climax-clock/ending-1/ending-5 use it directly). I re-checked every other word in both the closed-syllable-words and castle-key-words sets letter by letter and confirmed none of the others (lock, chest, clock, key, stage, exit, gate, coin) contain b, d, p or q, so this is a single-word problem, not a broader pattern failure. I also want to correct the scope of an earlier claim: narrative-designer's work/revision-notes.r3.md section 4 says 'stage', 'gate', 'clock' and 'coin' also contain b/d/p/q alongside 'steps' -- I re-checked all four letter by letter and none of them do; only 'steps'/'step' is actually at fault. This issue was raised as a major finding in review-2-literacy.r2.json, acknowledged by qa-engineer (qa-review.r2.json) and by narrative-designer (revision-notes.r3.md section 4, which states narrative-designer has no authority to swap a word-weave-plan-mandated word and explicitly asks for it to be escalated to product-architect/continuity), yet two revisions later (r3, r4) it is still open, and I find no corresponding entry for this job in workflow/work-items.json, so there is no tracked ticket forcing the escalation to happen. None of the automated checks catch this because it is not a taxonomy concept mismatch -- 'steps' correctly carries the closed-syllable pattern it is grouped under; the problem is the brief's separate, bespoke b/d/p/q promise, which my role as the dyslexia specialist is the right place to keep raising. Recommending changes-requested again until product-architect either (a) replaces 'steps' in brief.json's closed-syllable-words list and continuity.facts with a genuinely b/d/p/q-free closed-syllable word (for example 'mask', 'nest', 'last' or 'rock'), with word-weave-plan.json and the draft rebalanced to match, or (b) explicitly amends continuity.facts to document 'steps' as a deliberate, acknowledged single exception to the no-b/d/p/q rule, so the story's own design claim is no longer self-contradicting. Either fix is a brief/continuity-level decision outside narrative-designer's authority, per their own revision-notes.r3.md.
findings.passage: brief.json#continuity.facts; drafts/story.r4.json closed-syllable-words set (e.g. path-b-find: "The steps will show the way out."; climax-clock: "showing steps down and out"; ending-1: "went down the secret steps")

findings.message: reports/validation.r4.json's brief check reports a warning, '1 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 13-word limit' (maxSentenceWords: 13), while reports/literacy.r4.json's own sentence-length automated check only tests a fixed 20-word threshold and so shows 0 violations -- the same detection-limit gap I flagged in review-2-literacy.r2.json. I hand-split every paragraph in drafts/story.r4.json into sentences and found the warning is a tokenizer artifact, not a real violation: the only paragraph a naive splitter miscounts is path-a-find's "Finn said, 'This must unlock something.' Suri put the key in her coat.", which a period-plus-whitespace splitter treats as one 14-word run because the sentence-ending period sits inside a closing quote mark before the next capital letter. Read correctly it is two sentences of 6 and 7 words. I found no sentence over 13 words anywhere in the draft by hand count. Flagging only so the 13-word warning is not mistaken for a real issue, and as a second data point that the automated sentence-length check's fixed threshold does not track brief.maxSentenceWords.

Word-set minimums, coverage and naturalness: hand-verified against the draft text, not only trusted from the report. sh-words totals 40 against a minimum of 10, closed-syllable-words totals 42 against 30, castle-key-words totals 60 against 40; every word in all three sets appears at least once (missingWords: [] for all three, confirmed by reading the passages); and each set appears on the shortest route to every one of the five endings (reports/literacy.r4.json perEndingRoute has a nonzero count for every set on every ending, and I traced the graph by hand: opening and the-gate are on every route and alone carry all three sets, since the-gate's paragraph uses 'lock', 'clock', 'EXIT' and 'Steps'). The words read naturally in context rather than as a drilled list -- for example 'shelf', 'chest', 'key' and 'coin' are concrete story props (the chest in path-a-find, the shelf of old notes in path-b, the key and coin found together) that the plot genuinely needs the reader to track across branches, and 'rush'/'shut'/'wish'/'hush' are ordinary verbs and short exclamations embedded in dialogue and action beats (Theo wanting to 'rush' ahead, 'a hush fall[ing] over the three of them') rather than inserted as isolated vocabulary drill.

Skills practised: read start to finish on any route, this story gives repeated decoding practice with short-vowel closed-syllable words (lock, chest, steps, clock) and the sh digraph (wish, shine, flash, crash, shelf, rush, hush, shut, shock) in natural sentence and dialogue context, plus heavy, naturally-repeated exposure to a small set of plot-critical sight words (key, stage, exit, gate, coin) that the reader must recognise quickly to follow the plot rather than decode fresh each time. The branching structure built around finding an inventory item (the key and coin) and a clue (Wren's note), then choosing whether to set the clock or turn the key first, gives practice in sequencing a short ordered set of steps and in inference (working out that the key and the note are meant to be used together, and what each possible order of operations costs or saves). The short glossary entries with syllable breakdowns (castellan, theater, curious, furious, founder) support vocabulary growth from context. Across the whole story, the deliberately small, controlled, highly repeated word list lets a developing reader meet the same words often enough, across the opening, both search branches, the gathering point, the gate, the climax and all five endings, to build fluency with them rather than meeting each only once.

Limits of automated detection, stated per this job's requirement for every review: reports/literacy.r4.json and reports/literacy.r4.md both say their method is deterministic token counts plus ORTHOGRAPHIC (spelling-pattern) detectors, not phonological ones -- a detector match means a word's letters fit a regex, not that a qualified human has confirmed the sound a reader would actually produce (the report's own example: 'ea' matches both 'bread' and 'bead'). I independently re-ran the actual closed-syllable and digraph-sh detectors from src/literacy/taxonomy.ts by hand against every word-set word in this revision (see the first finding above) rather than trusting the report's conceptMismatches: [] on its face, because that same field silently hid a real defect on revision 2 when a 'concept' key was simply missing from one word set. Minimum-occurrence counts, every-word-used and per-route coverage are reliable deterministic counts and I independently spot-checked those against the draft text; they are not in question. The b/d/p/q letter-reversal issue raised above is outside what any automated check in this repository looks for at all -- it is a bespoke accessibility promise in this brief's own theme text, not a taxonomy concept, so only a human or careful manual reading catches it. I am an AI-assisted reviewer, not a certified literacy professional; a qualified human should confirm the phonological and decodability judgements in this review before publication.

The sole major blocker from my revision-4 review (literacy-review.r4.json finding 2) is resolved. brief.json's theme now reads '...and nearly every noun or verb the story leans on again and again was chosen to have no b, d, p or q in it at all. The one deliberate, documented exception is "steps": it is the story's central escape-route object and was kept for its closed-syllable decodability, a conscious trade-off against the letter-reversal goal for this single word, not an oversight.' and continuity.facts now reads '...contain no letter b, d, p or q; short, hard-to-avoid function words like and, had and said may still appear. The single documented exception is "steps", the central escape-route object, kept despite its "p" because closed-syllable decodability took priority for this one word.' Neither sentence makes the old blanket 'contain no letter b, d, p or q' claim unqualified any more; both now name 'steps' explicitly as a conscious, acknowledged exception rather than an unstated contradiction. I compared this wording byte-for-byte against generation-prompt.md's normalized-brief block and request.json's continuity.facts entry and both carry the identical corrected sentence, so the fix is consistent across all three files, not just brief.json. The design claim is no longer self-contradicting. I also checked the 'avoid' list's forward-looking instruction ('do not introduce a new recurring... word that contains b/d/p/q... never a repeated or tracked word'): this reads as guidance for words the author might add later, not retroactively over 'steps', which is a pre-mandated word-weave-plan word that predates and is now explicitly carved out from that rule; I see no residual contradiction here worth blocking on, but flag it so a future reviewer knows I considered it.

findings.message: Word-set minimums, concept classification and route coverage re-verified fresh on revision 5, not merely carried over from my r4 sign-off. reports/literacy.r5.json: sh-words 40/10 (minimum), closed-syllable-words 42/30, castle-key-words 59/40, missingWords: [] and conceptMismatches: [] for all three. These are within 1 occurrence of the r4 totals (sh-words 40 in both; closed-syllable-words 42 in both; castle-key-words 60 -> 59, key 24 -> 23), which matches the only textual change in this revision: narrative-designer's rewrite of two ending-5 sentences removed one incidental 'key' token ('Without the key and the note...' became 'Trying it alone...') while the closing sentence still carries 'key' ('...try the key and the note together'), and 'steps' is untouched at 10 occurrences in both revisions since the edited passage (ending-5) never contained it. I re-ran the taxonomy's closed-syllable detector by hand on lock/chest/steps/clock and the digraph-sh substring check on all nine sh-words words again against the current word lists in brief.json and word-weave-plan.json (word-weave-plan.json's sha256 is unchanged from r4, confirming the plan itself was not touched) and confirm the same result as r4: all declared words genuinely carry their declared concept, and castle-key-words is correctly left without a concept field (key/stage/exit/gate/coin still don't share one taxonomy pattern -- gate/stage are silent-e, key is an untracked 'ey' spelling, exit is two syllables, coin is an untracked diphthong). reports/weave-comparison.r5.json confirms both target-concept sets (sh-words, closed-syllable-words) meet their minimums against the word-weave-plan's planned/actual counts. Every set still appears on the shortest route to every one of the five endings per literacy.r5.json's perEndingRoute (all nonzero).

The same tokenizer-artifact warning I flagged on r4 persists unchanged on r5: reports/validation.r5.json's brief check still warns '1 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 13-word limit' while literacy.r5.json's own fixed 20-word sentence-length check shows 0 violations. This is the identical, already-diagnosed false positive from path-a-find's "Finn said, 'This must unlock something.' Suri put the key in her coat." -- a naive period-plus-whitespace splitter counts it as one 14-word run because the sentence-ending period sits inside a closing quote before the next capital letter; read correctly it is two sentences of 6 and 7 words. Repeating this note only so the warning is not mistaken for a new or real issue on this revision.

Spot-checked the unrelated ending-5 fix narrative-designer made this revision (not a literacy-review requirement, but noting it since I read the full diff). The two rewritten sentences in ending-5 ('Trying it alone, the lock would not give way.' and 'They never did open Wren Castellan's secret way out. Next time, they would try the key and the note together.') read as natural, state-agnostic prose rather than a drilled word list, keep 'lock' and 'key' in ordinary sentence positions, and introduce no new vocabulary outside the existing glossary. I see no literacy regression from this change.
